messages.subject: Re: variable effort point transect analysis
messages.subject_clean: variable effort point transect analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Anna,

It's not a multiplier you need - multipliers just multiply or divide the
total density by a scalar value.  What you want is to put the amount of
effort into the "Survey effort" field that Distance automatically
creates in the "Point transect" layer.  This field normally has a value
of 1 for each point, indicating that each point was surveyed once.  If
you surveyed some points twice, say, you just enter a 2 for those
points.  If you're getting data into Distance via the data import
wizard, as is recommended, then you just need a column in your input
file for effort.  Hope this helps -- but if I haven't been clear than
email me direct, off the list.  Cheers,

  - Len Thomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

That box (on Step 5 of the New Project Setup Wizard) is for the case

when you want to apply the same multiplier to all samplers, and its

value is known with no error.  Examples include: one sided transects

(e.g., surveying from one side of a plane or submarine), where you'd

enter 0.5 in the multiplier record once it's created; surveys where you

did the same number of visits (>1) to each point or line, where you'd

enter the number of visits.  In Anna's case she said she has different

effort for each point, so the way to handle that is to enter the effort

(number of visits) in the point transect layer, in the field that

Distance creates for this.  Cheers, - Len

Dear Distance software users,

Further to my message of 20th November (copied below), our paper on
Distance has now been published, and is now the default citation for the
software.  The citation is:

Thomas, L., S.T. Buckland, E.A. Rexstad, J.L. Laake, S. Strindberg, S.L.
Hedley, J.R.B. Bishop, T.A. Marques and K.P. Burnham. 2010. Distance
software: design and analysis of distance sampling surveys for
estimating population size. Journal of Applied Ecology 47:5-14.

The paper is freely available to everyone under an OnlineOpen agreement
with the publisher, and copies can be downloaded from the publisher at
  http://www3.interscience.wiley.com/journal/122685866/abstract
or
  http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2664.2009.01737.x
or from our local university repository at
  https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/handle/10023/817

If you have any problems obtaining a copy, please email me.

We suggest in your write-ups you continue to be explicit about the
version and release number of Distance you used, since results may vary
between versions. For example, you might write in a methods section:
  "Analyses were carried out using Distance 6.0 release 2 (Thomas et al.
2010)"

We will update the "Citation" page of the Distance manual with the next
release.

Best wishes to all,

  - Len Thomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,
I am currently using DISTANCE to analyse data from line transect surveys
of rainforest birds.  My general aims are to relate community structure
to environmental variables such as climate.  My sampling is stratified
across both latitude and elevation, with my interest being in
contrasting the density of different species in my strata and relating
that to the environments in these strata.  My use of the distance
approach is motivated by the problem of comparing count data between
locations with potentially different habitat structures, such as across
an elevational gradient, because of the potential for the shape of
detection functions to vary, biasing the estimates of density.  While
all my surveys are in rainforest, and as such the habitat variable is
somewhat controlled, I would like to be able to test if this assumption
is correct., hence my applying the DISTANCE method.   Apologies if this
as an obvious question,  and please recommend some further reading for
me if that will suffice (!) but I am searching for a simple explanation
of how to use DISTANCE to compare not the /estimated densities/, which I
expect will vary according to the environmental preferences and spatial
distribution of the species, but the shape of the function itself, which
I assume (perhaps erroneously) will remain constant where conditions are
constant (despite actual changes in density of species), and will vary,
eg where habitat is more dense or the canopy lower.  Any thoughts would
be much appreciated.
regards

Alex Anderson

Have a look at the golf tees sample dataset that comes with Distance.

messages.body_plain:
Dear list,=20

I'm seeking clarity on what happens to the estimator for detection probabil=
ity when distance data exhibit movement away from the line. Think I grasp t=
he concept, but must be missing something fundamental and can't resolve wha=
t's going on. Here's my understanding and where I'm getting lost.=20

I have line transect data from aerial surveys at sea. As expected, when usi=
ng many fine grain distance intervals to inspect data for such problems, th=
ere is evidence of evasive movement away from the flight path for a surplus=
 of detections in 2nd or 3rd distance class, depending on choice of interva=
ls to group data. (If it helps, my data look somewhat like the Adelie pengu=
in data with ten distance classes, Fig 3 in Fewster et al 2008 'Influence o=
f animal mobility.." Using 30 m distance bins, the data exhibit effect of e=
vasive movement on the part of Adelies. Using 60 m bins masks the effect (F=
ig 4).)

I understand that responsive movement prior to detection can lead to failur=
e of the uniform assumption. My understanding is that an overestimation of =
detection probability - positive bias in the estimator for detection - can =
 lead to an underestimate of object density. Meanwhile an underestimation o=
f detection probability - negative bias in the estimator - can lead to over=
estimation of density. So for a scenario, if g(0) < 1 but you proceed as th=
ough g(0) =3D 1, then estimator for detection will be biased high since the=
 estimator 'assumes' you've seen more than you have. And this translates in=
to an underestimation of density because the ultimate compensation for what=

 you detect should have been much larger.

What I'm stuck on is what happens when there is a dearth of distances at/ne=
ar the line, e.g., in the first distance class, followed by a surfeit of di=
stances in the 2nd/3rd class and then a fairly well-behaved drop-off after =
that out to w.=20
I thought that when the estimator for detection probability is biased high,=
 then density estimate will be too low. And if estimator for detection is b=
iased low, then density will be too high. In the 2001 Distance book p. 32: =
=93If evasive movement occurs prior to detection, the estimator will be bia=
sed low.=94   The section goes on to say that for the less common type of r=
esponsive movement, when animals move toward an observer, a positive bias i=
n estimated density can be expected. So I infer for that case that the esti=
mator for detection must have been biased low. =20

But is there a contradiction here? Or maybe I'm just hung up on when the es=
timator for detection or estimated density is being talked about. My basic =
question is what happens to the estimator for detection probability in the =

case of movement away from the line and why?
Sorry for the long-winded query, thanks greatly for any help!

Robin Hunnewell

Robin-

Easy way to think about it is that N=3Dn/p so if p is lower than it shoul=
d=20
be then N is higher and vice versa because N is based on reciprocal of=20
p.  Density is just N divided by area so same concept applies.  Why is p=20
too high with movement away from the line?  Think about it as stretching=20
out the area you are sampling.  Imagine a scenario in which you saw 100%=20
in one bin and 50% in the next farther equal-sized bin.  If 1/3 of those=20
in the first bin moved into the second bin and you detected 50% of them,=20
then your observed bins would have equal numbers of detections and your=20
estimated detection probability would be 1.0 (because it is scaled to=20
the origin being 1) when in fact the average was truly 0.75 had they not=20
moved.  The opposite occurs when you have movement towards the line.  If=20
half of the ones in bin 2 moved to bin 1 then the relative number of=20
observations would be 150% and 25%.  Rescaling these to 1 in first bin=20
would yield an estimated detection probability of (1+25/150)=20
/2=3D.583<0.75.  Note that this is all conceptual and the models are not=20
fit by scaling in this fashion -- only conceptually.

Fortunately you have movement away from the line which is the less nasty=20
of the two types of directed movement.  It is better because the bias is=20
such that you'll get an underestimate of abundance (p is too high) and=20
that is better for precautionary management. But it is also better in=20
that it will not always lead to bias or at least much bias.  To be=20
honest I haven't read Rachel's paper thoroughly and I should (sorry=20
Rachel) but I worked on this subject for my MS and those results are=20
summarized in the Burnham et al Wildlife Monograph on Line Transect=20
Sampling.  There are also other subjects on this matter.  Bottom line:=20
if your responsive movement is such that if only animals close to the=20
line move away but are still seen then you'll get little bias because=20
the curve fitting will "smooth" and "average" across those intervals. =20
You will see a lack of fit obviously.

Now here are two problems.  1) A lack of observations in the first few=20
bins may be movement or it may be that they were simply missed.  Are you=20
working with flat windows on the side of the aircraft?  If so it is well=20
known that observers don't like to look straight down and that can be=20
the case even if you have bubble windows.  See Ch7 of Intro to Distance=20
Sampling. 2) You can't truly discern whether or how much movement is=20

messages.subject_clean: Effect of movement away on detection probability
messages.body_plain:
Robin-

Easy way to think about it is that N=3Dn/p so if p is lower than it shoul=
d=20
be then N is higher and vice versa because N is based on reciprocal of=20
p.  Density is just N divided by area so same concept applies.  Why is p=20
too high with movement away from the line?  Think about it as stretching=20
out the area you are sampling.  Imagine a scenario in which you saw 100%=20
in one bin and 50% in the next farther equal-sized bin.  If 1/3 of those=20
in the first bin moved into the second bin and you detected 50% of them,=20
then your observed bins would have equal numbers of detections and your=20
estimated detection probability would be 1.0 (because it is scaled to=20
the origin being 1) when in fact the average was truly 0.75 had they not=20
moved.  The opposite occurs when you have movement towards the line.  If=20
half of the ones in bin 2 moved to bin 1 then the relative number of=20
observations would be 150% and 25%.  Rescaling these to 1 in first bin=20
would yield an estimated detection probability of (1+25/150)=20
/2=3D.583<0.75.  Note that this is all conceptual and the models are not=20
fit by scaling in this fashion -- only conceptually.

Fortunately you have movement away from the line which is the less nasty=20
of the two types of directed movement.  It is better because the bias is=20
such that you'll get an underestimate of abundance (p is too high) and=20
that is better for precautionary management. But it is also better in=20
that it will not always lead to bias or at least much bias.  To be=20
honest I haven't read Rachel's paper thoroughly and I should (sorry=20
Rachel) but I worked on this subject for my MS and those results are=20
summarized in the Burnham et al Wildlife Monograph on Line Transect=20
Sampling.  There are also other subjects on this matter.  Bottom line:=20
if your responsive movement is such that if only animals close to the=20
line move away but are still seen then you'll get little bias because=20
the curve fitting will "smooth" and "average" across those intervals. =20
You will see a lack of fit obviously.

Now here are two problems.  1) A lack of observations in the first few=20
bins may be movement or it may be that they were simply missed.  Are you=20
working with flat windows on the side of the aircraft?  If so it is well=20
known that observers don't like to look straight down and that can be=20
the case even if you have bubble windows.  See Ch7 of Intro to Distance=20

occurring from your observed data because it is a product of animal=20
distribution and detection.  If animal distribution is not uniform you=20
can't truly infer anything about detection and vice versa.  If you have=20
double observers you can make some inference about detection=20
independently which could enable inference about movement.  I gave an=20
example in my MS (probably in monograph as well) in which you can mix=20
movement away from the line and a steep detection function and get=20
observed data that looks like it should with a shoulder.  You should ask=20
yourself whether Adelie's could move the distances that you think they=20
are in the time the aircraft passes and when they would have to respond=20
to move that distance.

Hope this helps. --jeff

Hi all!

I have point count data from 2 breeding seasons, each point only visited
once.  I am wanting point-level density estimates to use in a regression on
habitat variables.  I first used model selection to compare effects of
covariates.  Then I used the top model to estimate density.  In the
estimates tab, I checked the boxes to estimate density and detection
function by global and sample (as a preiovus post reply indicated).  This
method does not seem to produce the right results - several points with
detections have no variance around them.  When I only use the global
detection function, the results are more reasonable and include variance.
However, no variance is calculated for those points with no detections.
Since there is a probability of not detecting a bird that is present,
shouldn't there be a predicted density estimate for every point.  Do I need
to calculate variance using the bootstrap method?

Thanks for any help!

Jennifer Reidy
